chunks: Data memory vs program memory. The question: What is the difference between data and program memory?
Program memory holds the instructions a CPU follows. Data memory holds the values those instructions work on, such as variables and buffers.
The difference is mostly about role: instructions are read in order, while data is read and written all the time.
Some chips keep the two in separate memories, and others share one memory for both.
Picture trucks crossing a river. Instruction trucks bring the next step to the CPU. Data trucks bring or take away the numbers it works on.
With one shared bridge, the trucks take turns, so a data truck makes an instruction truck wait. With two bridges, both cross at the same time.
The shared bridge has one advantage the picture hides: you can use its space for whatever you need, with no fixed split.
Left, one bus carries both instruction fetches and data traffic, so they must take turns.
Right, two buses let the CPU fetch the next instruction while the current one reads or writes data.
Program counter (PC): the CPU's bookmark, holding the address of the next instruction to read. Load/store: instructions that read data from memory or write data to it.
Harvard architecture: separate memories and paths for instructions and data. Von Neumann architecture: one memory and one path shared by both.
CPI: the average number of clock cycles (ticks of the chip's timing beat) each instruction takes.
An ATmega328P microcontroller is a Harvard chip. It has 32 KB of flash (memory that keeps data without power) for the program and 2 KB of SRAM (fast memory that forgets) for data.
Now take a simple processor that reads one instruction per cycle, where 30% of instructions are loads or stores.
With one shared memory, each load or store blocks the next instruction fetch for one extra cycle. So CPI equals 1 plus 0. 30 equals 1. 30 . With separate memories, CPI stays at 1.

"Program memory holds the instructions the CPU fetches with the program counter; data memory holds the variables and buffers the instructions load and store.
Program memory is mostly read-only at run time and often non-volatile flash, while data memory is read/write, usually SRAM.

In a Harvard architecture they're physically separate so you can fetch and access data in the same cycle; in von Neumann they share one memory and bus, which is more flexible but creates a bottleneck.
Modern CPUs use split L1 caches over a unified main memory."
